narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven first by your class ranking at the end of your third year, which placed you in the bottom decile. This was the single strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile, was the second most important factor and similarly increased the likelihood of failure. These two academic-standing measures outweighed everything else in the decision.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. Because it is only modestly below the average of accepted students (37.2), it slightly improved the model’s outlook, yet not enough to overcome the effect of your low class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9, middle-income background, full-time study plans, gender, and race played far smaller roles; the model focused overwhelmingly on your school performance and test score.

To strengthen future applications, you should retake the LSAT and aim for a noticeably higher score, or consider a post-baccalaureate program that would allow you to demonstrate stronger academic performance before reapplying. Improving those two areas gives you the clearest path to shifting the prediction in your favor. (218 words)
